clue.text: Tradesman accommodating a person’s husband’s old bike

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room to, so one piece is housed inside another

blocks.note: a baker is a tradesman who sells bread
'one's' is the possessive of 'one', a person in general
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper keeps hold of somebody's husband's ancient bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a person's' is the impersonal possessive, as in 'one's own'; 'accommodating' puts the person and husband inside the tradesman.
explanation.definitionFit: Boneshaker is the nickname for early bicycles with rigid frames and wooden wheels that gave a jarring ride.

clue.text: Finally invest in extra memory storage space

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of a word, so only its closing letter is used
placing something in another means it ends up enclosed

blocks.note: in cricket a bye is an extra, a run not scored off the bat
last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Advice to spend at last on more computer memory.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a run gained without the batsman hitting the ball counts as an extra; a bye is one kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A byte is the basic unit of computer memory, eight bits holding one character of data.

clue.text: Not a talking bird left — so-called!

blocks.note: no as a negative
the mina, or myna, is an Asian starling that mimics speech
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone protests that the bird that departed was not really a talking one, merely called that.
explanation.walkthrough: MINA is a recognised variant spelling of myna.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nominal exists in name only, which is what calling it so-called implies about the label.

clue.text: Oddly, she bred pigs at first in quiet part of London

indicators.note: done oddly means done in a strange way, so the letters come out in a strange order
at first points to the opening of a word, so only its initial letter counts
being in something means being surrounded by it

blocks.note: shush is a call for quiet
taken as written
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A woman strangely raises pigs in some peaceful corner of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like it wants odd letters, but here it signals the anagram; 'quiet' is a whole word meaning hush, not just P or SH.
explanation.definitionFit: Shepherd's Bush is a district of west London, home to a large shopping centre and the old BBC Television Centre.

clue.text: Like stars mostly missing on lake

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: something gone astray is missing
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Celestial bodies largely absent above a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: ASTRAY drops its last letter and L follows; 'on' sets the lake after it in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral is the adjective from the Latin for star, meaning relating to or resembling the stars.

clue.text: One tests former partner, a 27

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
taken as written
27-across is COLLIER, a coal miner

explanation.surface: Someone checks up on an ex who works down the pit.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference sends you to 27-across, whose answer means a coal miner; use its sense, not its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An examiner is a person whose job is setting and marking tests, so the phrase describes the role.

clue.text: In Strasbourg, who quietly makes a sarcastic gibe?

blocks.note: qui is French for who, and Strasbourg is in France
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: A question about which person in an Alsace city mutters a snide remark.
explanation.walkthrough: A foreign city is the crossword cue to translate the next word into that country's language.
explanation.definitionFit: To quip is to make a witty or cutting remark, and a sarcastic gibe is that kind of remark.

clue.text: Seizer of power taken in by loan shark

indicators.note: being taken in by someone means being received inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for power
a usurer lends money at exorbitant interest

explanation.surface: A would-be ruler is swindled by a predatory moneylender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seizer of power' reads as one phrase, but the definition is the single word and 'of' links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurper grabs a throne or authority by force or without right, so the word names one who takes it.

clue.text: Possibly Mac’s benefactor, ultimately busy with microphone

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: a patron gives financial support
last letter of the word
mic is short for microphone; 'with' joins it on

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's sponsor is finally kept occupied with a microphone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mac's' reads as possessive, but the 's is 'is'. 'Possibly' flags Mac as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Mac means 'son of' in Gaelic surnames, so it is a prefix naming someone after their father, an example of that category.

clue.text: Storm arising from key politician interrupting trial

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: E is a musical key
MP stands for Member of Parliament
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: An uproar caused by an important MP disrupting a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'key' looks like an adjective meaning important; here it is the musical key E.
explanation.definitionFit: A tempest is a violent windy storm, the literary word Shakespeare used for his play's title.

clue.text: Rough up an old sailor in sound

indicators.note: in sound means as heard, so the spoken form is what counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: an old salt is an experienced sailor

explanation.surface: Beating up a veteran seaman, phrased as an order or a news line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old salt' is the idiom for a seasoned sailor; said aloud with a weak 'a', the phrase matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To assault someone is to attack them physically, and to rough up is to beat someone up.

clue.text: Could it be an elder’s part, to snore away thus?

definitions.text: Could it be an elder’s part, to snore away thus?

blocks.clueFragment: an elder’s part, to snore away
blocks.note: surface reading: an older person dozing loudly

blocks.clueFragment: Could it be an elder’s part
blocks.note: setter's reading: the elder is a tree, and a piece cut from a tree trunk snoozes in the idiom

explanation.surface: Wondering whether snoring away is what old people do.
explanation.walkthrough: The elder is a shrub or tree, not an old person; the idiom compares deep sleep to an inert chunk of timber.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to sleep very soundly and motionlessly, like a felled length of wood lying still.

clue.text: An ancient country imports it as a provider of heat

indicators.note: to import is to bring goods in from abroad, so one piece is brought inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
Thrace was an ancient region of south-east Europe
taken as written

explanation.surface: A historic nation brings in something to serve as its fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: Thrace lay in the Balkans, across parts of modern Greece, Bulgaria and Turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthracite is hard, high-carbon coal that burns hot with little smoke, so it is a fuel.

clue.text: In favour of reducing support

indicators.note: reducing a word makes it shorter, so its last letter is cut

blocks.note: a prop is a support

explanation.surface: Backing a policy of cutting state support.
explanation.walkthrough: PROP loses its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro is the Latin-derived word meaning for, as in the pros and cons of an argument.

clue.text: Is Trotter able to get a supporter for light holders?

blocks.note: 'Is ... able' turned into a question is 'Can ...'
Del Boy Trotter is the hero of the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses
completes 'Is ... able', already given
taken as written
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: Can a character from a sitcom acquire a backer for his candlesticks?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is Trotter able' is the question 'Can Del'; Del Trotter is the wheeler-dealer of the BBC sitcom Only Fools and Horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Candelabra are branched candlesticks, each holding several candles, so they hold lights.

clue.text: Attraction of every part of a Yorkshire river

blocks.note: every part is all
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: The appeal of every stretch of a northern English river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure flows through Wensleydale and Ripon in North Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Allure is the quality of being powerfully attractive or tempting, a charm that draws people in.

clue.text: Leader of jaguars spotted cat heading off unknown risk

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so the first letter is taken
with its heading off, a word has lost its top, its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of the word
the leopard is the classic spotted big cat
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A chief jaguar sighted a big cat setting out into unknown danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spotted' looks like a verb meaning seen; it describes the cat. X, Y and Z are the algebraic unknowns.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeopardy means danger of loss or harm, as in putting a job in jeopardy, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Protagonist in drama — quite unlike Leander!

blocks.note: first meaning: a central character lacking heroic qualities
second meaning, read cryptically: Leander swam the Hellespont nightly for love of Hero, so his opposite would be against her

explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Leander loved the priestess Hero; someone 'anti Hero' is the reverse of him. The capital H is hidden by the answer's form.
explanation.definitionFit: An antihero is a lead character in a play or novel without conventional heroic virtues such as courage or nobility.

clue.text: Lining up for vinaigrette, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: in drill, troops are ordered to align their ranks in a straight row
second meaning: a sauce poured over salad, of which vinaigrette is one example

explanation.walkthrough: The military sense is the less familiar one: 'right dress!' orders troops to straighten their line.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both aligning a row of troops on parade and the oil-and-vinegar sauce added to salads.

clue.text: Rats, maybe, not very visible ultimately with trace of dark in fur

indicators.note: not means without, so those letters are taken away
ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter is used
a trace is the smallest hint, so just one letter, the first, is used

blocks.note: rats are an example of vermin
V is the abbreviation for very
last letter of the word
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Rodents barely seen, with a dark tinge to their coats.
explanation.walkthrough: VERMIN without its V, then E and D.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermined means trimmed or clothed with ermine, the white winter fur of the stoat worn on ceremonial robes.

clue.text: Resort having edge in Italy originally

indicators.note: originally means at the origin or start, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: a rim is an edge
taken as written
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A seaside town with an advantage over others in Italy at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having edge' suggests an advantage, but edge is simply a rim.
explanation.definitionFit: Rimini is a popular beach resort on Italy's Adriatic coast, so it is an example of a holiday spot.

clue.text: Assume this person’s opposed to MDMA

blocks.note: 'this person' is the setter, I, and I'm is 'I am'
agin is dialect for against
MDMA is the drug ecstasy, slang E

explanation.surface: Take it that I am against the party drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this person' means the setter; the 's is 'is', making I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: To imagine can mean to suppose or take something to be true without proof, as does assume.

clue.text: Good luck symbol firm introduced to staff

indicators.note: something introduced to a thing is put inside it

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
a mast is a pole or staff

explanation.surface: A company's charm is presented to its employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees; it is a pole, as in flagstaff.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a person, animal or object adopted to bring a group good fortune, a lucky emblem.

clue.text: Hit hosted by school, a musical

indicators.note: a guest hosted by others is inside their home, so the letters sit within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the ending of the first word, the second, and the opening of the third

explanation.surface: A hit show staged by a school, a musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' looks like a box-office success, but it is a verb meaning strike.
explanation.definitionFit: To lam is an informal verb meaning to beat or thrash someone hard, so it means strike.

clue.text: What some school leavers may hope for, almost entirely one-sided

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut

blocks.clueFragment: What some school leavers may hope for
blocks.note: uni later: going on to university after school
entirely means all

explanation.surface: Pupils hoping for something nearly wholly biased.
explanation.walkthrough: Uni is British shorthand for university.
explanation.definitionFit: Unilateral describes action taken by one party alone, without agreement from the other, hence partial.

clue.text: Dash off fleetingly to get cheese

indicators.note: off means removed, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: to fly is to dash, hurry
briefly means for a short time

explanation.surface: Pop out for a moment to buy some cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash off' reads as hurry away, but the dash is the letters removed from the word for fleetingly.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft creamy French cheese with an edible white rind, named after the region of origin.

clue.text: Woman in bar — start of embarrassing howler

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
being in something means being enclosed by it

blocks.note: she is a woman
to bar is to ban
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A woman in a pub makes a shameful blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: The bar here is a prohibition, not a pub. 'howler' looks like a gaffe, but it means something that howls.
explanation.definitionFit: In Irish folklore a banshee is a female spirit whose wailing foretells a death, so she wails.

clue.text: Breed of dog right for an underground worker

blocks.note: the collie is a sheepdog breed
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A dog breed suited to someone who works below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the far end after the link 'for'.
explanation.definitionFit: A collier is a coal miner, someone who digs coal in a pit beneath the surface.

clue.text: Assistant’s proposal, sending head of army to front

indicators.text: sending head of army to front
indicators.note: sending the army's head, its letter A, to the front means moving that letter from the back of the word round to its start

blocks.note: an idea is a proposal

explanation.surface: A helper's plan to send the army chief to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: The A at the end of IDEA is the head of army; moving it to the start gives the answer. The 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An aide is a helper or assistant to someone senior, such as a political or military official.

clue.text: European left university visitor lacking time and energy

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: port is the left side of a ship
U is the abbreviation for university
a guest is a visitor
T is the abbreviation for time
E is the abbreviation for energy; 'and' adds it

explanation.surface: A continental departed from a campus guest with no time or energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' applies only to time; 'and energy' adds E. 'left' looks like departed, but it is the nautical port.
explanation.definitionFit: A Portuguese person is a native of Portugal, a country in south-west Europe, so is an example.
